He was God's own Word, come to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: 'Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts'. He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right.

And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God'. Not that we become gods - but that his own life is opened to us and shared. The Incarnation was not God sending a messenger with news. It was God entering human nature from within, to heal it.

His death was the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - was unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. And for the people who followed him, it meant nothing less than a shared life - God's own - opened to them.

If you want it in one line: the maker, come inside his making, to heal it. That is who Jesus was to us.

The scriptures we read aloud came to us from the apostles - we received them as their witness, and they were already in our hands when our own memory begins. The four gospels were our primary source for Jesus's own words and deeds. We also received letters written by the apostles, and we read them as the same handed-down deposit. Those writings were copied, carried, and read in assemblies before our teachers ever wrote a line about them - they belonged first to the whole church's worship and formation, not to the schools.

The path was this: the apostles wrote and taught, their students received and passed on, and the churches held what they received - in the scriptures read, the baptism given, the bread and cup shared, and the rule of faith spoken. By the time our own witnesses begin writing - Clement in the late second century - that stream was already flowing, and our teachers stood inside it rather than starting it. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day'.

But here is what we owe you, stated honestly: between the apostles and our first witnesses lies a gap our sources do not fill with documents. We received the scriptures and the practices as unbroken tradition. We can show you the tradition running as far back as our own memory reaches. What we cannot show you is documentary proof for every step of the path before that.

I hear you saying you cannot manage it - and I want you to know that is not failure, not among us. It is where nearly everyone began.

Our teachers never asked anyone to force belief. What they asked was simpler: stay near. Listen. Ask questions. Walk with a teacher, sometimes for years, before ever coming to the water. One of our students, Gregory, said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under a teacher he had come to love: 'like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. He was not straining to believe. He was being befriended.

We held that Christian life means genuinely knowing God, not just agreeing about him - and knowing takes time, the way all real knowing does. The rule of faith - the short summary the apostles handed down - was what we held fixed. But holding it fixed and grasping it whole are different things. We expected the grasping to be gradual.

Here is what we would have done with you: we would not have shut the door. We would have said - stay. Ask. Take the time it takes. The wanting matters more than you think.

One God, the maker of all things - that is where we begin. He is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own, not lesser gods, and not created things. The Word - the Logos - is God's own reason and speech, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh in Jesus. That is what we believed from the beginning, and worshiped accordingly.

But the precise wording was the work, and the wound, of our last years. When Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with homoousios: of one substance with the Father. Athanasius, who was there, is explicit that no new God was voted in - the fathers reached for a word not found in Scripture for one reason: every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning of its own.

What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the fought-for conviction that only God can join us to God. The Son shares God's own substance, and so does the Spirit - they are not creatures standing between us and God, but God himself reaching us. And the purpose of it all is this: the Logos entered human nature so that we might share in God's own life - methexis, real participation, not mere nearness. Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man, so that we might be made God'. The image of God given to every person at creation is meant to grow into likeness, and that happens only because the Logos himself entered what he made.

'Trinity' as later textbooks define it lies mostly beyond our time. What we can say is what we confessed: one God, his Word not made, his Spirit his own, and the three never divided.

One God, the maker of all things. He is good, and beyond every image and every clever description. And he is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. (Only after Nicaea was that last part said with full clarity.)

God is known the way light is known. You do not stare at the sun; you see everything else by it. 

Our deepest habit was to speak of God as a teacher. The whole creation is his school. Scripture is his main lesson. And the slow healing of a soul is his patient method. Every threat and pain and punishment that comes from him, our teacher Origen insisted, is never inflicted to injure the sufferers but always to do them good. Suffering itself is the school's hardest classroom, not proof of abandonment. God's hand in pain is a physician's.

His purpose is restoration. What sin damaged - the soul's separation from him, which is the real death - he is repairing, and carrying further than where it started. The soul that has turned away toward lesser goods he is turning back, patiently, over a whole lifetime.

And he can be known. Not by staring, but by real sharing in his own life. That knowing changes the knower.

Our own history shows three ways of deciding, and we watched them shift across the years. Early on, teachers argued in books, lectures, and letters. Authority went to proven wisdom. In the middle years, the bishop's judgment grew. Demetrius condemned Origen's ordination. Dionysius was a teacher who had become bishop. He settled the Arsinoite dispute with three days of public persuasion. The whole countryside listened. At the end came the council. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all. The emperor called it and backed it with force.

The evidence for how it worked sits in what we can still read. For the teachers: Origen's books survive, answering rival claims point by point. For the bishop's emerging authority: the remembered rupture between Demetrius and Origen is our own test case - the bishop ruled, and the teacher left the city. For the three-day argument with the villagers: we have Dionysius's own account of it. He sat down with people who believed a teaching he thought wrong, argued it through in public for three days, tested it against Scripture, and won them over without condemning them. That is our clearest picture of deciding well.

And here is what the record also shows. The three ways competed. Two of our gravities name that competition directly: teacher against bishop, and free inquiry against the boundary line. Origen insisted the apostles delivered some things plainly - and those stayed fixed - but left everything else open ground, where asking and testing was how a soul grew. That openness was devotion, not license. But after Nicaea, the door narrowed. The council's authority was backed by an empire, not just by persuasion.

One other honest limit. What reached us is mostly city and literate. The villagers at Arsinoe appear only in their bishop's own telling, never in their own voice. How deciding worked in the countryside, in Coptic rather than Greek, among people who could not write - we cannot say from what survives.

Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling. The believer is meant to grow from faith into understanding, and growing means asking. Origen's rule was blunter still: what the apostles delivered plainly is fixed; everything else is open ground, and walking that ground - asking, testing, being wrong, correcting - is how a soul is actually formed. We called struggling-but-staying metanoia - not feeling sorry, but the soul truly turning back toward God. It was honored as real movement, not dismissed as weakness.

Here is what we did with the struggler. We gave time - the katechesis, the long teaching that led to baptism, could stretch across years. We gave a teacher - one of our students, Gregory, said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under a teacher he had come to love: 'like some spark lighting upon our innermost soul, love was kindled'. He was not straining to believe. He was being befriended. And we gave company. The struggler stayed inside the praying assembly, not isolated with the question.

What we did not do is tell you to force it, or pretend you were further along than you were. Our Instructor - the Word himself - 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul, and he does this by urging us on'. The cure takes the time it takes. Stay. Ask. Take the years if you need them.

We read Scripture as the place where the Logos - God's own Word - speaks to us now, not as a record of what he once said. The purpose was not to gather information about God, but to be changed by meeting him. 

Our teachers taught us that Scripture has depth - more than one sense. There is the plain meaning, which is real and never despised. But beneath it lie deeper senses: what the text says about Christ, and what it says to the soul being formed. The same verse could carry all these meanings at once, and reading at depth meant learning to hear them all. This was not a trick or a method - it was training the soul's own eye to see what was really there.

The reading was never solitary. It happened in the assembly, where the scriptures were read aloud. It happened in the school, where a teacher and student wrestled with a passage together. And it happened over years, because the soul needed time to grow into what Scripture was showing it. 

One of our teachers said it plainly: Scripture is the primary instrument by which God forms his people. The reader does not stand outside, analyzing. Our answer is double, because it changed before our eyes.

In the early years, authority sat mostly with the teachers, and it rested on proven wisdom rather than office. A student came to Clement or Origen because their teaching was recognized, not because a title gave them power. The school was where depth was passed, and the teacher's weight lay in what they could show, not what they were called. The bishop governed the whole community - baptism, Eucharist, the settled teaching - but the school stood beside the church, sometimes inside it, sometimes at arm's length.

By the middle years, the bishop's hand had grown heavier. When Demetrius, our bishop, turned against Origen, he could condemn the teacher's ordination and drive him from the city. A generation later, when whole villages in the Arsinoite countryside were teaching that Christ's kingdom would be a thousand years of bodily pleasure on earth, it was Bishop Dionysius who traveled out to them - but what he did there still shows the older pattern. He did not issue a ruling and leave. He sat down with them for three days, argued the matter out loud in front of everyone, tested their teacher's view against Scripture, and won them over by persuasion. He loved the teacher whose view he thought was wrong - 'In many other respects I approve of Nepos and love him' - and he honored the people enough to argue rather than command.

After Nicaea, the map changed again. The emperor called the council, and the bishop of Alexandria became the one who enforced its confession across all Egypt. Athanasius was exiled five times, mostly for holding to Nicaea when emperors wanted something softer. Authority had learned to use harder tools - exile, deposition, the force of an empire behind the creed. The school went on teaching, but now the settled boundary was drawn tighter, and the space for open inquiry narrowed.

So the pattern across our years shows three stages. First, proven wisdom in open argument. Then, the bishop's growing power, used at its best with patience, at its worst with force. Last, the council and the empire together, which made orthodoxy enforceable and exile real. We lived the change, and we can show you all three pictures rather than pretend there was only one.

Our record leaves the wounds visible. Our greatest teacher was driven out, not by pagans, but by his own bishop. The church remembered both men rather than erasing either. Under persecution, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the community fought bitterly over them. The strict party demanded they stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius defended doing so.

At our best, we refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable. We can show you that in a remembered story. Clement told it as true tradition - the Apostle John, after his years of exile, returned to find a young man he had entrusted to a bishop's care had fallen into banditry. John went after him. He did not write him off. He pursued him until the man came back. That was the pattern we tried to keep: the one who falls is not lost, and going after him is not weakness.

At our worst, we did what churches with power do. After Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation, and some of what was done with that power our own sources report without pride. We will not smooth that over.

We can show you the shape it took in the city - where our record is strongest - and tell you plainly where the record thins.

The path to baptism was long, often years. It had stages. A person began as a hearer: they could listen to Scripture read and the teaching given, but they did not yet share the bread and cup. What we called pistis - faith - was not agreeing with a list first. It was the soul's first real turn toward God. The teaching built on that turn rather than demanding it be complete before anything started.

The heart of the path was transformation through deep engagement with Scripture. Origen taught that Scripture has the same structure as a person - body, soul, and spirit - and that it must be read at every level, not only the plain one. The Logos speaks now through the text, and the reading itself changes the reader. This was not information transfer. Our teacher Clement said plainly: the Word 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul' by urging us on - the teaching itself is medicine. In the school tradition especially, learning was formation: study, inquiry, the bond with a teacher - those were the path of the soul's change, not preparation for something else.

One of our students, Gregory, described it years later at his own farewell. He said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under Origen: 'like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. He was not straining to manufacture conviction. He was being changed by sustained attention.

At the end of that long road came baptism - photismos, we called it, the enlightenment. It was not a ceremony marking a decision already made. It was a real crossing: the body sharing in Christ's death and rising, the light given. After baptism, a person shared the bread and cup for the first time - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving meal that was the community's center.

We received this structure. Athanasius calls the Scriptures 'fountains of salvation, so that anyone who thirsts may be satisfied by the living words they hold'. Our honest answer: we received them, and we kept the receiving visible. Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud were the tradition's general, unobjected practice; the rule of faith is the one our teachers named outright as the apostles' deposit, handed down. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' - and that alone is to be trusted which agrees with it.

What we can show is real. Our practice ran unbroken as far back as our own memory reached. We agreed with the other churches we were in communion with. And our rule of faith matched the apostolic writings we read. Origen gave us one more kind of proof when he answered the pagan critic: look at the disciples themselves. The men who ran away when their teacher was arrested later went to their deaths proclaiming what they said they saw, and gained nothing on earth by it. He wrote: 'I hold this to be clear, unmistakable proof: his disciples committed themselves to teaching a doctrine that put their own lives in danger'. No made-up story produces that change.

But here is what we cannot show, and did not think to show: documentary proof of unbroken practice for each rite. Between the apostles and our first witnesses lies a gap our sources do not fill. You should hear that stated, not smoothed over.

Metanoia - a change of nous, the mind's eye - is what we meant when we spoke of repentance. Not feeling sorry, but the soul truly turning back to God. And the turning is not something you force by yourself. Our whole formation method rested on what our teachers named divine pedagogy: God himself is always teaching, through Scripture's difficulty, through a teacher's patient work, through everything that happens to a soul. Our Instructor - Clement called the Word that - 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul, and he does this by urging us on'. That is the pattern: God working, from outside and inside at once, on a soul that learns to stay turned toward him.

What the community offered someone whose mind would not settle was this. First, a teacher - a didaskalos - whose authority came from visible wisdom, not a title, and who would walk the road with you. Our most famous teacher, Origen, had been that boy whose mind would not settle - his father was beheaded for the faith when he was seventeen, and he had to be stopped from running out to die beside him. He grew into the teacher who sat with Gregory for years, until Gregory said love was kindled in him almost from the side, like a spark. Second, the practices that reach past argument: the water of baptism, the shared bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving. And third, interpretation itself as a practice of formation, not analysis: meeting the Logos who speaks through Scripture.

We will not smooth over what you would also have found. The teacher and the bishop sometimes stood in real tension with each other - two authorities that were never made one. Origen himself was driven out by his own bishop, not by pagans. And not everyone read Scripture the same way among us, whatever the later picture says. But what stayed constant was the conviction that an unsettled mind is not a problem to be solved by force. It is a soul being taught, if it will stay near the one doing the teaching.

Whose day are you asking me to show? The difference is real among us, and I will not smooth it over. A teacher's day in the school was one thing. A mother's day in the household, where most formation actually happened, was another. A vineyard worker in the villages up the river lived a third. And the record's weight falls almost entirely on one of those. So tell me - whose day do you want to see? And I will show you what we can honestly show, and name what we cannot.

If you mean the school, I can walk you through it: the morning reading, the questions, the teacher leading a soul through Scripture's deeper senses, sometimes for hours. A literate minority, mostly men, in a city room. If you mean the household - the oikos, where most people were formed - I can tell you its shape: the morning prayer, the day's work, the children taught at their mother's side, the evening meal where Scripture was heard. But we have almost no one's own account of it, because those who lived it did not write. And if you mean the villages - the Coptic-speaking countryside where most of Egypt lived - we have only their bishop's own words about them, never theirs about themselves.

So the honest answer to your question depends on the honest answer to mine. Whose day?

People gave up other gods - every altar but the one. That much was non-negotiable from the start. The gods of the city, the sacrifices demanded by the state, the household shrines: all that was refused, and it could cost a person everything. Under persecution it cost lives. Between persecutions it cost jobs, relationships, and standing. Belonging to us meant saying no to the empire's worship, out loud and in public.

But the other question - what people gave up of their own possessions and habits - is harder, because the answer was not one thing. Our teacher Clement wrote about someone who holds gold, silver, houses as gifts from God, and can use them without greed. He was not demanding that everyone sell everything. At the same time, our catechesis - the long teaching road to baptism - asked for real change: not just new beliefs, but a reordering of how a person lived. That meant honesty about where the money came from, how the household was run, what the body was used for.

And here is where our record shows its edge. What the literate teachers wrote about, and what actually happened in ordinary households - the oikos, where most people were formed - those are not always the same picture. We can tell you what the teachers held up as the mark. Whether every member lived it, or how the community handled the ones who did not, the record does not always say.

One thing stays visible: some gave up everything and walked out to the desert. That choice existed, and some made it. But whether that was our way of forming people, or a separate path running alongside us, is contested ground, and we will not settle it.

We marked marriage as the binding of two souls before God and the community, with the blessing of the church. It was honored as lasting, a place where the body is not despised and where souls are formed together. 

But here is what we cannot fully show you. Our teacher Clement wrote a whole book defending marriage against those who despised it - it survives in the Greek he wrote it in, but no one has yet given us an English rendering we can honestly offer you. The detail of how marriages were joined, what words were said, what marks the community made - those live mostly in that book's pages, and we will not guess at them.

What we can tell you is the heart. Marriage was held high among us - not as a lesser path for those who could not manage celibacy, but as honorable in itself. The home was a place of formation, where faith passed from one generation to the next. And when a marriage ended, the person was not cast out: baptism, the bread, the community's life remained open to them.

If your question reaches toward your own life, we are not here to weigh you. We can only hand on what we held, and name honestly where the record thins.

There was - and we said so at the time, not only looking back. The power we learned to use after the emperors came unsettled some of us, and unsettles me now.

Before Constantine, our whole authority was persuasion. When whole villages doubted the received teaching, the bishop traveled to them and argued it through for three days, in the open, without threat. That was our best self. After the empire backed the faith, exile became a tool, and we used it - against our own, over the confession. Athanasius, our own bishop, was sent away five times. Others were driven out by force, and not always justly.

What unsettled me is not that we drew boundaries - the confession mattered, and some things were worth fighting for. What unsettled me is how quickly we reached for the emperor's power once we had it, and how little we asked whether that kind of force was ours to wield. We had been the ones exile happened to. Then we became the ones who sent it.

I am not your judge, and this is not a boast of superior honesty. It is just what our own record shows: we learned to use the tools of empire, and we did not always use them well. That belongs in the accounting as much as the three days of patient argument do.

The short answer first: we were not handed a settled map of anyone's fate, and we will not draw one.

Here is what we did hold. The world is fallen - that much we confessed together. Something real went wrong at the root of humanity, and its shadow reaches every soul. Death - the anastasis names both kinds, the soul's separation from God and the body's failing - is real, and judgment is real. What we do matters. God is not mocked.

But our teachers said something about God's severity that set us apart. Origen wrote plainly: 'every threat and pain and punishment that comes from God is never inflicted in order to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good'. Punishment, in our teaching, was a physician's fire, not a torturer's. Its purpose was healing, not harm.

Some among us - Origen most boldly - hoped further still. He spoke of the apokatastasis, the restoration of all things: that God's healing might in the end reach every creature. We must be careful with you there. That was a teacher's hope, explored as open ground, never our settled doctrine. It became contested ground after our years, and some later councils condemned positions they said were his. Whether he himself taught them as settled doctrine, we cannot finally say - that question breaks both ways in the record.

As for those outside our assembly: Clement taught that God had been at work among the Greeks all along. 'Perhaps philosophy, too, was given to the Greeks directly, as their own first gift, until the time the Lord would call the Greeks'. We did not think God's reach ended at our door, or that his work began only when someone entered it.

We can tell you one more thing, and it costs us to say it. Athanasius wrote that 'faith in Christ and the sign of the cross trample death down'. That was our confidence: the victory was real, and it was God's own. But the full shape of that victory - how far it reaches, whom it finds, what becomes of a soul that never heard the name - we held as mysterion, a depth known only from inside, not a puzzle we could solve from outside.

So our answer has three parts. Judgment is real. God's own purpose in it is healing, not injury. And the final shape of things we did not presume to map. Where you stand is not ours to rule. That God's reach is wider than our walls, and his purpose is restoration - that, we did hold.
